title: Can assistive listening technology improve hearing after subarachnoid haemorrhage?
official: Improving hearing and speech perception-in-noise after subarachnoid haemorrhage
summary:
Background and study aims
Some people who have had a subarachnoid haemorrhage have difficulty understanding speech when there is background noise, for example in restaurants, group conversations, meetings or other busy environments. This can happen even when standard hearing tests are normal.

This study aims to better understand this type of hearing difficulty after subarachnoid haemorrhage and to test whether an assistive hearing device can improve hearing in everyday noisy situations.

The device being tested is the Phonak Roger system. It includes a small receiver worn near the ear and a wireless microphone that can be placed near the person speaking. The system is designed to make speech clearer in background noise.

Who can participate?
Adults aged over 18 years may be able to take part if they have previously had an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, and have normal standard hearing tests but evidence of difficulty with speech perception in noise.

What does the study involve?
Potential participants will first complete screening questionnaires about hearing and listening difficulties. Those whose answers suggest difficulty understanding speech in noise will be invited to a face-to-face appointment at the University of Southampton.

At this appointment, the research team will examine the ears, perform standard hearing tests, test hearing in background noise, collect clinical and demographic information, and ask participants to complete questionnaires about hearing, quality of life and mood.

If the assessment confirms that a participant is eligible, they will be randomly allocated by chance to one of two groups:

Device group: participants will receive the Phonak Roger system and will be shown how to use it in everyday situations where hearing speech in noise is difficult.

Control group: participants will not receive the device and will receive standard care, consisting of advice about managing speech perception-in-noise difficulty.

Participants cannot choose which group they are allocated to.

The main follow-up visit will take place after 3 months and will include repeat hearing tests and questionnaires. Further follow-up will take place at 6, 12 and 18 months. These later follow-ups will usually be completed remotely, for example online, by telephone or by post.

Participants allocated to the device group may be offered the option to keep the device after the trial has finished but will be responsible for device maintenance.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may or may not benefit directly. Those allocated to the device group may find that the device helps them hear speech more clearly in noisy situations, but this is not guaranteed. The study may also help improve care for people with hearing difficulties after subarachnoid haemorrhage in the future.

The study is considered low risk. The hearing tests and questionnaires are non-invasive and are commonly used in research and clinical practice. The device is commercially available and is considered low risk.

Taking part may involve some inconvenience. The face-to-face visits may take up to 1–2 hours and may be tiring. Some questionnaire questions ask about hearing, mood, anxiety, depression, cognition and day-to-day functioning, which some people may find mildly upsetting. Participants can take breaks, stop an assessment, or choose not to answer any question they do not wish to answer.

Participants allocated to the device group may find the device unfamiliar or mildly uncomfortable, or may need time to get used to using it in daily life. Support will be available from the research team, and participants can stop using the device at any time.

Reasonable travel expenses for study visits may be reimbursed up to a maximum of £40 per visit, with receipts.

Where is the study run from?
The study is sponsored and run from by the University of Southampton. Face-to-face visits will take place at the University of Southampton. The University Hospital Southampton will be a patient identification centre.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
July 2026 to January 2030. The study is expected to run for 3.5 years. Each participant will be followed up for 18 months after joining the trial.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by Sonova. Sonova is also providing the Phonak Roger devices used in the study.

Who is the main contact?
i-hear@soton.ac.uk
conditions: Speech perception-in-noise hearing difficulty following subarachnoid haemorrhage .
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage confirmed by CT or lumbar puncture and angiographic evidence of an aneurysm, three or more months post-ictus
2.	Adult (age >18 years)
3.	English-speaking
4.	Able to provide consent
5.	Difficulty with speech perception in noise despite normal peripheral hearing, i.e. a normal audiogram (based on HHIA, SSQ-12 and BKB adaptive SoNo score cut-offs as follows: HHIA: 18+, SSQ-12: ≤ 8.0, BKB adaptive SoNo: >-4dB)
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Any neurological condition affecting the brain other than subarachnoid haemorrhage
2.	Any language condition affecting communication and the ability to complete the questionnaires and do the audiological testing
3.	Peripheral hearing loss and/or middle ear dysfunction
